language_wrapper: A row of {n} coins lies left to right. Their initial orientations repeat every {p} positions according to the string {pattern}, where H denotes heads and T denotes tails. A move consists of flipping a contiguous block of exactly {block_size} coins. On the first move, you may flip any such block wholly inside the row. On each subsequent move, the leftmost coin of the block you flip must be adjacent to the leftmost coin of the block you flipped on the previous move (we do not consider a position to be adjacent to itself). Determine the smallest possible number of moves required to reach a state in which every coin is heads-up.
hardness_rationale: Compared to the seed problem, this generalization requires flipping contiguous blocks of fixed size rather than single coins, and keeps the adjacency constraint by tying moves to the leftmost index of each block. Two layers of complexity arise: (1) a parity invariant on the total number of heads (it changes by block_size mod 2), which makes solvability itself nontrivial to certify; (2) finding the shortest walk of block-left endpoints that achieves the desired flip-parity on every coin is a constrained optimization problem over walks in a one-dimensional state graph with nonlocal effects. Even for the path graph, this becomes a vertex-parity walk problem that typically demands parity-invariant analysis and dynamic programming (or carefully reasoned constructive sweeps), rather than the simple sweeping strategy of the seed. Special cases (e.g., block_size=1 and alternating pattern) reduce to the seed with the known answer 2(n−1), but for block_size≥2 the optimal sequence is genuinely more intricate.
notes: Proof sketch of correctness for the verifier: Model the sequence of moves by a walk of leftmost indices on the discrete line {0,1,...,n−block_size}. Each step flips exactly the b=block_size coins covered by that block, so the coin-state vector over GF(2) is updated by XOR with the block's indicator vector. The global parity of heads changes by b mod 2 each move, so if b is even and the initial count of heads has opposite parity to n, the all-heads target is unreachable; the verifier enforces this invariant. Among all solvable instances, breadth-first search over states (coin mask plus last block-left index) explores all admissible move sequences in order of increasing length and therefore returns the minimal length when the all-heads configuration is first reached. The state space is finite, and adjacency is enforced by restricting successors to the two neighbors of the current leftmost index. This BFS thus computes the exact minimum number of moves. Connection to the seed: when b=1 and the initial pattern is alternating starting with tails, the optimal strategy is to sweep from one end to the other and back once, yielding 2(n−1) moves; this is the seed's solution. In the generalized setting with b≥2 and general periodic patterns, one needs to balance parity constraints and endpoint-walk planning, which is strictly more involved than the seed.
source_question:
The Bank of Pittsburgh issues coins that have a heads side and a tails side. Vera
has a row of 7873 such coins alternately tails-up and heads-up, with the leftmost
coin tails-up.
In a move, Vera may flip over one of the coins in the row, subject to the following
rules:
• On the first move, Vera may flip over any of the 7873 coins.
• On all subsequent moves, Vera may only flip over a coin adjacent to the coin
she flipped on the previous move. (We do not consider a coin to be adjacent
to itself.)
Determine the smallest possible number of moves Vera can make to reach a state in
which every coin is heads-up.
